title: PixiJS 3D batches ordinary meshes, and it shows everywhere
body: PixiJS 3D draws 1,000 separately animated meshes in 130 draw calls on WebGPU (9 on WebGL2), where every other engine issues 1,000. In Chrome on WebGPU it keeps 65,800 such meshes inside a 60 fps frame, against about 9,400 for PlayCanvas, 3,300 for Babylon Lite, 2,500 for three.js and 2,300 for Babylon.js. The same design carries over to sorted transparency (15,900 meshes against 6,800 for PlayCanvas, and 31,800 on WebGL2), to skinned characters (2,900 crossfading Foxes against at most 930 for the others) and to a 100,000-mesh world (2.4 ms a frame). In Safari it holds about 27,200 moving meshes on both backends.

title: Instancing still makes the engine choice almost irrelevant
body: Through each engine's instancing or batching path, with the hierarchy flattened by hand, all five sustain between 87,000 and 133,000 moving meshes at 60 fps in Chrome on WebGPU. That is 14 to 49 times what three.js, PlayCanvas, Babylon.js and Babylon Lite manage with one scene-graph node per object. Defold is the exception: 1.13.1 cannot draw instanced models on WebGPU, so it holds 3,600 there, and on WebGL2 its instances are still game objects moved from Lua (10,800, against 99,000 and more for the others' WebGL2 renderers).

title: Spawning is where Babylon.js hurts
body: With 20 of 2,000 meshes destroyed and recreated every frame, each with a new material and texture, Babylon.js spends 30 ms of CPU on a typical frame in Chrome, far over the 16.7 ms budget; in Safari the same frame takes about 220 ms. PixiJS 3D takes 3.6 ms, Babylon Lite 4.4 ms, PlayCanvas 9.8 ms and three.js 13 ms. three.js's WebGPURenderer has the worst single frame apart from Babylon.js (41 ms); its classic WebGLRenderer peaks at 8.7 ms. No engine built pipelines during the churn and in Chrome none grew GPU memory, but Babylon.js's JavaScript heap grew by 24 MB after a forced collection, and in Safari its GPU memory grew by 2 MB.

title: Many lights: three.js needs its clustered add-on even for 31
body: Sponza with cascaded shadows and 31 moving point lights costs three.js 45 ms a frame on WebGPU and 87 ms on its WebGLRenderer, nearly all of it GPU time in forward shading. PlayCanvas, Babylon.js and Babylon Lite put those lights on their clustered paths and PixiJS 3D shades them forward, and all four stay between 4 and 6 ms. With 256 lights three.js's clustered add-on is the fastest of all at 8 ms (Babylon.js and Babylon Lite 13, PlayCanvas 16). PixiJS 3D stops at 32 lights per view and three.js's WebGLRenderer has no clustered path, so neither can run that step.

title: A large world costs what exists, not what is visible, except in PixiJS 3D
body: With about 2,000 meshes in view, growing the world from 20,000 to 100,000 meshes doubles the frame in three.js (16 to 33 ms), nearly triples it in Babylon.js (28 to 74 ms) and more than triples it in PlayCanvas (5.4 to 19 ms), while PixiJS 3D stays at 2.4 ms. Each of the three has a static-world path that brings 100,000 meshes back to 5 to 10 ms, but you have to build it: BatchedMesh in three.js, hand-made instancing cells in PlayCanvas and Babylon.js. Babylon Lite does not frustum-cull ordinary meshes: at 20,000 it draws every one, and its frames arrive 296 ms apart in Chrome although its CPU and GPU pass times are 4 and 7 ms; in Safari it could not finish the camera path. Its GPU-culled thin instances handle 100,000 in 2.1 ms.

title: Crowds: Babylon.js's baked path is in a class of its own
body: With every character crossfading two clips, PixiJS 3D holds 2,900 Fox characters at 60 fps in Chrome on WebGPU, because its default path batches skinned characters (800 in 3 draw calls, 2 on WebGL2). Babylon Lite holds 930, PlayCanvas 590, three.js 550 and Babylon.js 360. For bigger crowds Babylon.js and Babylon Lite bake the animation into a texture and draw every character in one instanced call, each on its own phase, playing a single clip without the crossfade, a lighter workload. Babylon.js's baked crowd reaches 32,800 characters (15,400 on WebGL2). Babylon Lite's stops at 6,400: the next level needs a 25,600-texel animation texture, past the GPU's 16,384 limit. three.js and PlayCanvas have no first-party instanced or baked skinning, and PixiJS 3D's default path runs the single-clip crowd at 4,100.

title: Picking: the default call ranges from half a millisecond to 48
body: Picking one of 10,000 meshes costs 0.5 ms in PixiJS 3D and 0.7 ms in three.js, 4.5 ms in Babylon Lite, 7.5 ms in Babylon.js and 17 ms in PlayCanvas, whose only picker renders an id buffer for every pick. On a single one-million-triangle mesh the order flips: PlayCanvas 1.9 ms, PixiJS 3D 7.9 ms, the Babylons about 22 ms and three.js 48 ms, since no engine ships a BVH. The GPU pickers in Babylon.js and Babylon Lite take over 100 ms among 10,000 meshes, slower than their own ray picks, though Babylon Lite's picks the dense mesh in 2 ms; Babylon.js's reads the vertically mirrored pixel on WebGPU unless the caller flips y.

title: A HUD is cheap in PixiJS 3D and Babylon Lite, expensive in PlayCanvas and Babylon.js
body: Over the same 3D scene, PixiJS 3D keeps 9,000 moving nameplates at 60 fps in Chrome and Babylon Lite 2,600, and 500 nameplates add about 1 ms of CPU a frame to either. PlayCanvas's element components reach 547 and Babylon.js's GUI 393: 500 nameplates add 13 ms and 11 ms. Putting PlayCanvas's elements in batch groups triples its count to 1,700; Babylon.js's GUI has no batching path. In Safari on WebGPU, PlayCanvas's default UI already misses 60 fps at 250 nameplates. three.js handles 16,000, but it has no UI layer: that number is a hand-written quad batcher and canvas text, the largest file in its adapter.

title: Babylon Lite ships a tenth of Babylon.js
body: A minimal lit-cube app is 44 KB of brotli-compressed JavaScript with Babylon Lite, 104 KB with three.js's WebGLRenderer, 172 KB with its WebGPURenderer, 217 KB with PlayCanvas, 227 KB with PixiJS 3D and 422 KB with Babylon.js, counting every chunk each build emits. With glTF, animation, shadows and bloom, Lite and three.js both land near 195 KB and Babylon.js at 864 KB. Babylon.js is also the slowest to a first frame (313 ms for the cube against 48 to 66 ms for the others). Defold's engine is a fixed 0.8 MB on either backend (0.9 MB with glTF, animation, shadows and bloom), all of it downloaded before the first frame.

title: Defold: a fixed 0.8 MB engine, fast picks, a high price per object
body: Defold 1.13.1 runs from one build per backend: its stock WebGL2 engine, and the WebGPU one its editor builds from an app manifest. Either downloads about 0.8 MB before the first frame and draws the lit cube in 156 ms in Chrome on WebGL2 (267 ms on WebGPU), against 47 to 76 ms for three.js, PlayCanvas and PixiJS 3D. Every mesh is a game object moved from Lua: it holds 3,600 moving scene-graph meshes on WebGPU and 2,400 on WebGL2, where three.js's WebGLRenderer holds 9,100. Its physics ray casts pick among 10,000 meshes in 0.03 ms. They hit collision shapes rather than triangles, though: they agree with the exact pick on 53 of 64 points, and it cannot pick on a triangle mesh. On WebGL2 its instanced path holds 10,800 meshes and its GPU-skinned, instanced crowd 7,100 Foxes, second to Babylon.js's baked crowd (15,400). Its WebGPU backend is younger: it cannot draw instanced models yet, its GPU skinning fails WebGPU validation, so the crowd skins on the CPU and stops at 348 Foxes, and creating textures every frame costs 0.6 s a frame against 8 ms on WebGL2. Defold ships Lambert-only lights and no shadows or post-processing, so the Sponza steps that need them use render-script code written for this benchmark and are shown unranked, and a model plays one animation at a time, so the crossfading crowd is not applicable. Its GUI holds 1,500 moving nameplates on WebGPU (519 on WebGL2), 2,900 once its nodes are grouped in layers. Defold was measured in its own sessions two days after the others: in Safari the drift-check cell ran 7–8% faster than in the main run, so its Safari numbers may read up to that much better.

title: WebGPU is still not automatically faster
body: With one node per object, three.js's classic WebGLRenderer sustains 9,100 moving meshes where its WebGPURenderer sustains 2,500, and 7,300 sorted transparent meshes against 2,400. Babylon.js is also ahead on WebGL2 (3,900 against 2,300), and PixiJS 3D sorts twice as many transparent meshes there (31,800 against 15,900). PlayCanvas is about level on both. WebGPU's clear wins are the things WebGL2 cannot do at all: compute particles, clustered lighting in three.js, and Babylon Lite as a whole, which has no WebGL2 renderer.

title: Safari changes the ranking for Babylon.js, and its WebGPU has rough edges
body: Babylon.js's per-object cost is four to six times higher in Safari than in Chrome: it holds 541 moving meshes on WebGPU against 2,300 (645 against 3,900 on WebGL2), and its HUD scene is over budget before any nameplate is added. Its lit Sponza with 31 lights takes 198 ms on Safari's WebGPU, against 6 ms in Chrome and 4.4 ms on Safari's WebGL2. three.js, PlayCanvas and Babylon Lite land close to their Chrome numbers; PixiJS 3D drops to less than half (27,200 moving meshes) and still leads. One of Safari's WebGPU drift-check runs failed with 'Unable to make command encoder' and passed on every other repeat. Safari's frame interval sometimes exceeds what CPU and GPU pass times explain, so capacities there count the interval past 20 ms.
